newsitem.title: UK: RUGBY UNION-FRENCH STILL DETERMINED TO RULE THE ROOST.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-FRENCH STILL DETERMINED TO RULE THE ROOST.

text.p: Once a decade the French rugby team perform as reliably as any farmyard cockerel greeting the dawn in Dax. Thirty years ago, 20 years ago, 10 years ago...the Five Nations title has disappeared across the Channel each time and this weekend will determine if fate really is on the side of Jean-Claude Skrela's team.

Rarely before this season have any French side endured as many simultaneous injuries to key personnel, reflected by a line-up against Wales short of seven experienced internationals with more than 250 caps between them.

Emile N'tamack, Thomas Castaignede, Alain Penaud, Fabien Galthie, Philippe Benetton, plus long-term absentees Philippe Saint-Andre and Olivier Roumat, are all missing, a gloomy list to worry any coach before a test match.

"If it continues like that, I will have to put myself in the team," smiled Skrela, overlooking the fact he won the last of his 46 caps against Wales in 1978. Many French supporters would love to be transported back to the grand slam days when Paparemborde, Paco, Cholley, Imbernon, Palmie, Rives, Skrela and Bastiat ruled the forward roost, but even such legendary iron men might have buckled under the demands of modern rugby.

Internationals and European Cup matches, interspersed by the legalised mayhem of French domestic rugby, as team manager Jo Maso has acknowledged, have given players less and less time to recover from the big hits of the professional era.

Yet Skrela, a member of the French grand slam side in 1977, can still field a team with the potential to maintain their country's symmetrical record. The man he says he will miss most is Benetton, the Agen flanker who is recovering from surgery on a broken jaw.
"Even when you don't see him much, Philippe's so useful, especially in defence," he said. "Now it's up to Richard Castel to show he can do just as well."
The ultimate French test still looks likely to come at Twickenham against England on March 1, but they need only cast minds back to September to know what Wales are capable of.

In a friendly international in Cardiff the home side led 27-10 at halftime before two tries in the final six minutes salvaged the French a shaky 40-33 win. The Welsh have been significantly strengthened since then by the return of their rugby league contingent, to the extent that a first win in Paris since 1975 is not a complete impossibility.

Neither is an Irish win over England in Dublin, proof that the Five Nations championship is a weird and wonderful beast. Written off after home defeats to Western Samoa and Italy, the Irish have been revitalised since the appointment of Englishman Brian Ashton as coaching advisor.

Ashton left Bath after disagreements with former England international John Hall, who ironically also parted company with the club on Tuesday, and was gratefully seized by Ireland to replace New Zealander Murray Kidd.

His new players duly beat Wales in Cardiff by a single point two weeks ago and now encounter an English side who, despite their dramatic late three-try burst and record win against Scotland, are still struggling for consistency.
"I am the most patriotic Lancastrian and Englishman, but I will be as green as shamrock when England come to Dublin," said Ashton.

If he has half the success Jack Charlton managed with the Irish soccer team, the man now dubbed Brian O'Ashton will never have to buy a drink in Dublin again. On Saturday, he starts with the advantage of knowing all about opposite number Jack Rowell's methods from their days together at Bath.

England captain Phil de Glanville has called for Rowell to be reappointed through to the 1999 World Cup, but his predecessor Will Carling is more concerned with the threat the Irish always pose at home.

"If you don't get iron control they will knock you out of your rhythm and defeat you," said Carling. "Playing Ireland at rugby is always a headache, especially in Dublin, where you can have headaches on the pitch and a certain headache afterwards."
